batch_note: Yes, two templates predict the key. (1) Seven of the eleven textual items (A-01, A-03, B-01, B-02, C-01, C-03, D-01) share one option cast: the shared pattern restated, its reversal, and a reversed pair on the two groups named in the passage's 'however' sentence. The key is always the half of that pair where the named person's factor is present and the rival's is absent. A test-wise student strikes two options on form, and the 'however' sentence names the key's groups; after one item, the other six are recognizable. Only A-02, B-03, C-02 and D-02 break the cast, and they are the strongest textual items. (2) Seven table items (A-04, A-06, B-04, C-04, C-05, D-05, D-06) use the same template: 'X beats every member of group G', all four options share the subject's prefix, one lure comes from outside G with the closest value, and the key is the strongest member of G. The rule 'find G's best row' solves all seven, and the off-group lure is spotted on sight. Key letters are balanced (A6 B6 C7 D5), so this is a structural tell, not a positional one. All 24 keys match my cold answers.
